analysis.one_liner: Moves deferred mortgage payments to the end of the loan and pays landlords to waive rent and hold off evictions during COVID emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on January 4, 2021, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have protected homeowners and renters during declared COVID-19 emergencies. If a homeowner deferred mortgage payments, the bank could not demand repayment until the very end of the loan term, instead of shortly after the deferral ended. It also created a program giving landlords low-interest loans — forgiven if they extended leases and agreed not to evict — in exchange for waiving tenants' rent. It applied retroactively to the existing COVID emergency and to any future one. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who defer mortgage payments during a declared COVID emergency would get to repay them at the end of the loan rather than being hit with a lump-sum bill. Renters whose landlords join the program would keep housing without paying rent during the emergency, and eviction protection would extend 60 days beyond it. Landlords who waive rent would receive federal loans of up to half the waived amount, forgiven if they extend leases and refrain from evictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners and renters hit by COVID emergencies

how_it_helps.text: During a declared COVID-19 emergency, lenders could not demand repayment of deferred mortgage payments until the end of the loan term — so a homeowner who skipped payments would owe them at the end of a 30-year mortgage, not in a lump sum months later.
Landlords who waived tenants' rent could get quarterly government loans of up to half the waived rent, at no more than 4% interest and no fees.
Those loans would be forgiven entirely if the landlord extended leases and agreed not to evict any tenant until 60 days after the emergency ended.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and servicers would wait longer to collect deferred payments, losing interest and cash flow. Taxpayers would fund the landlord loan program, which authorizes unlimited appropriations. Landlords bear the condition of extending leases and delaying evictions to get forgiveness.

drawbacks.text: Mortgage lenders and investors would have to wait until the end of the loan term to collect deferred payments, losing the interest they would otherwise charge on early repayment — a cost banks and mortgage investors would push back on.

The Tenant Protection Program pays landlords up to half of waived rent with loans forgiven if they extend leases and hold off evictions, and authorizes unlimited appropriations — a costly, loosely capped use of federal money that partly channels relief through landlords rather than directly to tenants.
Applying retroactively to payments already deferred since the start of the declared emergency would force lenders and borrowers to rework agreements made under earlier rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — preventing deferred payments from becoming a lump-sum bill when homeowners are most vulnerable — is large for affected families. The costs are real but manageable: lenders lose interest timing flexibility, and the landlord loan program is a voluntary federal program with loan terms attached, open-ended in funding ("such sums as may be necessary"), which an honest supporter should acknowledge. The 4% interest cap and mandatory forgiveness are generous to landlords but come with anti-eviction and lease-extension strings for tenants.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, the first week of the new Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services that same day, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken.
It drew 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, and none in the Senate.
When the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers are better off, since they keep the ability to demand deferred payments on their own terms; renters facing eviction and homeowners with deferred payments got no protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage lenders; renters and homeowners unprotected

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Maxine Waters)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican backed it and no Senate companion was introduced.

industries.note: They could not force deferred payments to come due early; repayment would be pushed to the end of the loan term, costing them interest and cash flow. Their loss is the homeowner's gain.
The bill routes tenant relief through landlords: cheap, potentially forgivable federal loans for waiving rent. Landlords get paid while tenants get eviction protection for the emergency period.
Deferred-payment forbearance attached to the end of the loan term changes the expected cash flow on mortgage-backed investments, delaying returns.
